---
title: "5 · Unsupervised Learning I: Dimensionality Reduction, Clustering, Autoencoders"
code-tools: false
toc: false
---

Most scientific data come without labels. The first questions then concern the data themselves, namely which few variables describe a sample, whether the samples form groups, and which samples are unusual. Principal component analysis (PCA) gives every sample new coordinates along the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, the directions of largest variance. The method t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding) drops the linear map and places the samples in a plane so that neighbours in the data stay neighbours in the plane, which makes groups visible that a linear projection mixes. Clustering with k-means and DBSCAN (density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise) turns these groups into labels, and the silhouette score and the adjusted Rand index measure their quality.

An autoencoder learns its own compression. An encoder maps each sample to a few latent numbers, a decoder rebuilds the sample from them, and samples that are rebuilt badly are flagged as anomalies. We apply these methods to handwritten digits (MNIST), photographs (CIFAR-10) and blood cells, then to the detection of credit-card fraud and of an unseen tumour type from the expression of 20 531 genes. We return finally to the Ising model, where the first principal component turns out to be the magnetisation and an autoencoder trained without labels detects the phase transition.
